932.title: Harvest home
932.hook: harvest festivals and Thanksgiving mark the end of the year's work
932.carry: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy
932.howItsDone: At harvest festivals, churches and communities decorate with produce, sing harvest hymns and share a meal, and the gifts are sometimes given away; Thanksgiving brings families together around a shared table.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sukkot: a roof of branches, more shade than sun, and room for the stranger. Your line was the booth.

The last wagon of sheaves comes up the lane toward the barn, and the field is finally bare. In English country tradition, that moment had a name: harvest home. Tradition says a supper followed, for everyone who had worked the field, the farmer and the laborers at one table. The words made their way into hymns. In the United States and Canada, a Thanksgiving table can still carry some of that feeling: a season's work done, and a meal to mark it. Today: harvest home.
screen: `THE LAST LOAD COMES IN.` → `ONE TABLE FOR EVERYONE.` → `HARVEST HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the song. An English hymn by Henry Alford puts today's word in its second line: "Come, ye thankful people, come, Raise the song of harvest home: All is safely gathered in, Ere the winter storms begin." It celebrates not the profit but the relief: the work is done, and done in time. Second, the tears behind it. A psalm puts the harvest in a longer story. In the King James words: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." Some of the sowing happened in bad years and worried seasons. The joy at harvest is the same field, seen from the other end. Third, the full table. Deuteronomy pictures a people settled in a good land and eating their fill, and says, in the King James words: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee." The next verses warn why: a full house is where forgetting starts. So the thanks is set at the moment of plenty, not only in the lean years. Jewish tradition takes this verse as the root of the blessing said after meals. Fourth, your own field. You may never bring in wheat. But a year of work has a harvest too: a project finished, a child grown a little, a skill that wasn't there before, a hard season gotten through. And some of it may have been sown in tears. A harvest festival is a pause to look at what's gathered, call it by name, and give thanks, before the next season starts.

segments.voice: Look back over this year of your work, paid or unpaid, and let three things you've gathered come to mind: something finished, something learned, something survived. If one was sown in tears, let that be part of it, and picture someone who helped you bring it in. If you pray, give thanks in your own tradition's words; if not, just say thank you.

933.title: Pongal, the harvest
933.hook: a Tamil harvest festival thanking the sun and the cattle; the rice pot boils over for luck
933.howItsDone: At Pongal, Tamil families draw kolam patterns at the door, cook new rice with milk and jaggery in a new pot facing the sun until it boils over, call out "Pongalo Pongal", and honor their cattle on a day of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was harvest home: all safely gathered in, and a blessing at the full table. Your line was they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
screen: `THEY THAT SOW IN TEARS SHALL REAP IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Early morning in a courtyard in Tamil Nadu. A pattern of rice flour, a kolam, has been drawn on the ground outside the door. A new clay pot sits over a fire, facing the rising sun, with turmeric leaves tied around its neck. Inside: new rice, milk, and jaggery. The whole family is watching it. Nobody is stirring. They're waiting for the moment it rises to the rim and spills over the side. When it does, they shout. Today: Pongal.
screen: `A KOLAM AT THE DOOR.` → `A NEW POT FACING THE SUN.` → `EVERYONE WATCHING IT SPILL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Pongal is both the festival and the sweet rice dish cooked for it. Tamils keep it as the month of Thai begins, when the harvest is in, and it runs over several days. Second, the sun. The main day thanks the sun, Surya, for the harvest. The pot is set out in the open, facing east, and the first rice of the new crop is cooked and offered before it's eaten. The meal begins with thanks to the light the fields depend on. Third, the cattle. A day is set aside for the cows and bullocks that pulled the plows. They're washed, their horns are painted, they're hung with bells and flowers, and they're fed some of the sweet rice. The animals who did the work get thanked like workers, because they were. Fourth, the overflow. Tradition says the pot boiling over is a good sign, a picture of a household where good things spill beyond the rim. People call out Pongalo Pongal as it rises. Usually a pot boiling over is a mess to clean up. Here, it's the whole point. The Tamil classic, the Thirukkural, has a chapter in praise of farming. In paraphrase, one of its couplets says that however far the world wanders, it still follows the plow. Pongal is the day the world turns around and thanks the plow, the sun and the ox, and lets the pot run over.

segments.voice: Picture the pot on the fire, the milk rising slowly, the family waiting, and think of one good thing in your life sitting just under the rim: a thank-you not yet said, a compliment kept to yourself, some time or food you could share. Let it rise in your mind, and picture where it might spill over, and to whom. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for whatever feeds you.

934.title: Your work, written
934.hook: what is your work, really, beyond the job title?
934.howItsDone: People who write down their real work usually keep it to one plain sentence about what they do for others, put it somewhere visible, and revisit it when their work or stage of life changes.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Pongal: a pot of new rice left to spill, with thanks to the sun and the cattle. Your line was boil over.

So, what do you do? It's the first question at a party, and the easy answer is a job title. Accountant. Nurse. Student. Between jobs. Retired. The title is true, but it's thin. It doesn't say that the accountant is the one who stays calm when a family's finances fall apart, or that the student is quietly holding a household together. For weeks this path has looked at work through scripture, craft, festivals and harvest. One question is left: what is your work, really? Today: your work.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `THE TITLE IS THIN.` → `WHAT IS YOUR WORK, REALLY?`

segments.voice: First, an essayist on calling. Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay Spiritual Laws, puts it in two short sentences: "Each man has his own vocation. The talent is the call." A vocation, in his sense, isn't a title someone hands you. It's what you're fitted for, the one direction, he says, in which all space opens. A title can match it, or only sit somewhere near it. Second, a job description in one line. The prophet Micah sums up what God asks in a single sentence. In the King James words: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Three verbs, no job title, and it could sit on top of all sorts of jobs. Third, the gap. Between the title and the real work, there's usually a gap. A teacher's title is teacher; her work might be making sure no child feels stupid. A bus driver's title is driver; his work might be getting tired people home safely, and being a kind face at the end of a long day. The title is what's on the badge. The real work is what you'd want someone to say you did. Fourth, writing it down. One line is enough: short enough to remember, plain enough to check against a Tuesday. It isn't a mission statement for a boss. It's a sentence for you, and it can change as your stage of life changes. Emerson's was for anyone with a talent. Micah's was for a whole people. Yours only has to be true.
screen: `THE TALENT IS THE CALL.` · `DO JUSTLY, LOVE MERCY, WALK HUMBLY.` · `THE BADGE AND THE REAL WORK.` · `ONE LINE IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `YOUR WORK.`

segments.voice: Say your job title to yourself, then set it aside and ask: when my work is going well, what am I really doing for people? Let a few answers come and go, keeping things safe, making things clear, helping someone heal, or learn, or rest. Look for the truest one, and shape it into one plain line you could write down.
Your work. Not the title on the badge, but what you're really doing for people, written in one line. Today's word.

935.title: Service at work
935.howItsDone: Some Christians serve at food banks, hospitals and prisons with Matthew 25 in mind; in Islam, small acts of help count as sadaqa, charity; others look for service by naming who their everyday work helps.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was your work: the talent is the call, and Micah's three verbs beneath any job title. Your line was my real work.

Who is a spreadsheet for, at eleven at night? Or a line of code nobody will ever read, a pallet of boxes in a warehouse, a form stamped and filed? Some work seems far from any human face. Yet follow it far enough and there's usually someone at the other end. The spreadsheet decides whether a family's loan goes through. The code keeps a hospital's records from crashing. The boxes are somebody's birthday present. Today: Sahih al-Bukhari.
screen: `A SPREADSHEET AT ELEVEN.` → `FOLLOW IT FAR ENOUGH.` → `SOMEONE AT THE OTHER END.`

segments.voice: First, a surprise at the end of a story. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells of a king who welcomes people for what they did: they fed the hungry, gave the thirsty a drink, took in a stranger, visited the sick and the prisoner. They're puzzled. In the King James words: "Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee?" The king answers: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Christians read the least of these in more than one way. What the story itself stresses is the surprise: they served without knowing who was at the other end. Second, a hand with the luggage. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari lists small acts that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, counted as charity. In paraphrase: helping someone onto his animal, or lifting his bags up to him, is charity. A good word is charity. Moving something harmful out of the road is charity. None of it needs a title, just a person nearby who needs a hand. Third, the hidden line. Your work may not look like feeding the hungry. But the same thread runs through a desk job: somewhere down the line, a person is helped, or not, by how you do it. Naming that person changes the task. Fourth, the difference. A form filed for nobody is a chore. The same form filed so a widow gets her pension on time is service. The job hasn't changed. What changes is that you can see who's at the other end. In Matthew's story, the helpers never saw who it was. Today's practice tries to.

Notice whether the task looks any different with them there. Stay with them for a few breaths, holding them in your own tradition's words if you pray, or simply wishing them well.

936.title: Work as practice
936.hook: a task done with attention is practice
936.carry: fully there for the warm water and the plate
936.howItsDone: In Zen monasteries, monks and visitors do samu, a period of cleaning, gardening and kitchen work done in silence as meditation; Christians drawn to Brother Lawrence try to keep God in mind through ordinary tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sahih al-Bukhari: the least of these, and a hand with someone's bags. Your line was who it serves.

Before he ever cooked for monks, he was a footman, and by his own account a great clumsy fellow who broke everything. Later, as a lay brother in a Paris monastery, he was sent to the kitchen, work he says he naturally disliked. A few weeks ago, at the start of this block, this path met him there, in the clatter: Brother Lawrence. Now, something smaller he said, about an egg in a pan, and about what to do when the mind wanders off. Today: samu.
screen: `A CLUMSY FOOTMAN.` → `SENT TO THE KITCHEN.` → `AN EGG IN A PAN.`

segments.voice: First, the omelet. Brother Lawrence's letters and conversations were gathered into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God. In paraphrase, he says we needn't do great things: he turns his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. The size of the task isn't the point. And when he notices he has wandered, he doesn't scold himself or make a show of being sorry. He simply comes back. Second, the monastery work period. In Zen monasteries in Japan, there's a name for the hours spent sweeping, weeding, cleaning and cooking: samu, work practice. It isn't a break from meditation. It is meditation, with a broom. The attention given to the breath on a cushion is given to the corner of the floor. Third, the dishes. The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about washing dishes. In paraphrase: there are two ways to wash the dishes. One is to wash them to get them clean, so you can get on to the next thing. The other is to wash the dishes to wash the dishes, fully there for the warm water and the plate in your hand. Only the second, he said, is really being alive while you do it. Fourth, what makes a task practice. Not the task. A Christian cook, a Zen monastery and a Vietnamese teacher each speak from their own tradition, and each points at attention. Any task, done with full attention and coming back when you drift, can become practice. These weeks have asked why we work, and who for. This is about how.
screen: `A LITTLE OMELET, FOR THE LOVE OF GOD.` · `SAMU: MEDITATION WITH A BROOM.` · `WASH THE DISHES TO WASH THE DISHES.` · `PRACTICE IS ATTENTION.` · then, large: `WORK AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: For now, the breath is the task: follow it in and out, the way Brother Lawrence turned the omelet, just this one, now. When the mind drifts to something else, notice where it went and come back, without scolding, then come back again. The coming back is the whole exercise.
Samu. The Zen name for work practice: sweeping, weeding and cooking done with the same attention given to the breath. Today's word.
Your line: fully there for the warm water and the plate. Any task can become practice when you keep coming back. Day nine hundred thirty-six, done.

937.title: Different answers
937.hook: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work differently
937.carry: the part matters more than the applause
937.howItsDone: People on different paths describe their work through their own tradition's lens: some as a calling, some as an offering or a duty, some as an honest livelihood, and some as simply hard and necessary.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was samu: one ordinary task, done with your whole attention. Your line was fully there for the warm water and the plate.
screen: `FULLY THERE FOR THE WARM WATER AND THE PLATE.`

segments.voice: A lunch break, and five coworkers share a bench outside. Ask each what their work really is, under the job title. The first says: it's the price of being alive. The second: it's what I was made for. The third: I do it for someone else, not for me. The fourth: it's my part, and somebody has to do it. The fifth shrugs: it pays the rent, and I try to earn it honestly. Nobody on that bench is wrong. Over these weeks on work, each of those answers has turned up in a tradition on this path. Today, all five go side by side.
screen: `FIVE PEOPLE, ONE BENCH.` → `FIVE ANSWERS.` → `ALL FIVE, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the curse. In Genesis, outside the garden, the ground turns hard, and the King James words are blunt: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." Some readers hear a punishment there. Others hear plain honesty: work is hard. Second, the calling. Martin Luther taught that a milkmaid or a cobbler serving the neighbor is doing holy work, and the letter to the Colossians says: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Third, the offering. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever he does, eats or gives can be done as an offering. The work goes up like a gift, and the result stops being the point. Fourth, the duty. The Gita again: better your own duty done imperfectly than someone else's done well. Your work is your part, and the part matters more than the applause. Fifth, livelihood. The Buddha names trades to avoid, such as dealing in weapons and poisons: earn a living in a way that doesn't harm. These aren't five rival theories where one has to win. The Gita itself holds two of them, offering and duty, in one book. A nurse can call her work a calling and still feel the sweat of it after a night shift. And the answer can change with the season of a life, or the day of the week. On a Monday it's sweat. On a good Thursday, it might be an offering.
screen: `THE SWEAT OF THY FACE.` · `DO IT HEARTILY.` · `AS AN OFFERING, AS A DUTY.` · `EARN IT WITHOUT HARM.` · then, large: `MORE THAN ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Say the five words slowly to yourself: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood. Hold your own work up to each one, the way you'd hold a shirt up in front of a mirror, and notice which fits today, maybe two at once. If you pray, you can offer that word in your own tradition's way.
Different answers. Curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood: the traditions see work in different ways, and a person can hold more than one. Today's word.
Your line: the part matters more than the applause. Some days it's sweat, some days an offering. I'll keep a seat for you.

938.title: Work close
938.hook: sixty days on work, and the last move: finish, look, rest
938.howItsDone: Several traditions pair work with set times of rest: the Jewish Sabbath, Christian Sunday rest, Friday congregational prayer in Islam, monastic hours of prayer, and Buddhist observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different answers: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood, and room to hold more than one. Your line was the part matters more than the applause.

A carpenter sets down the plane, runs a palm along the tabletop, and steps back. Not to start the next job. Just to look. That small pause is where this whole stretch on work ends. It began with a garden that needed tending. Since then: a craftsman filled with spirit, a tentmaker, a farmer Guru, a woodworker who fasted before he carved, a Chan master who wouldn't eat on a day he didn't work. This week alone: a harvest, a written answer to what your work really is, service, attention, and five different answers. Today, the last move. Finish. Look. Rest.
screen: `STEP BACK AND LOOK.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON WORK.` → `FINISH. LOOK. REST.`

segments.voice: First, finishing. Back on day eight hundred eighty-six, Rabbi Tarfon said it isn't yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop. That's true of the big work: justice, a family, a life. But inside it are small things that can be finished. A drawer. A letter. Finishing one is its own kind of practice. Second, looking. Again and again in the creation story, Genesis pauses to look. At the end of the sixth day, the King James says: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." The work isn't over until someone looks at it. Not to find the flaw. To see it. Third, rest. The next verses don't start a new project: "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." In that story, rest isn't what's left when the work runs out. It's part of the shape. Fourth, the whole block in one line. The traditions gave very different answers about what work is. But across the texts on this path, one rhythm kept showing up: the Benedictine hours, the Sabbath, Friday prayers, the observance days. Work well, then rest. Ecclesiastes says there's a season for everything, "and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Work had its season here. Tomorrow a new question begins.
screen: `FINISH ONE SMALL THING.` · `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.` · `HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `WORK WELL, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `WORK WELL, THEN REST.`

segments.voice: Picture one small thing you could finish, one email, one shelf, one mended button, and see yourself doing it with care to the last step. Then see yourself stepping back, like the carpenter, just looking, no checking for mistakes, and let your hands rest in your lap. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the work of these weeks.
Sabbath. The end of sixty days on work: finish something, look at it, and rest. Today's word.
Your line: work well, then rest. The stopping is part of the shape. See you tomorrow.
